articles.title: States Turn to Innovative Solar Tenders to Create Markets Beyond Conventional PV
articles.description: India’s solar market is usually measured through large utility-scale projects, rooftop installations and increasingly battery storage. But a parallel trend is emerging across state government procurement: governments are using tenders to create demand for smaller, application-specific solar technologies that have yet to achieve large-scale commercial offtake. From concentrated solar cooking systems and solar water heaters to solar fencing, solar dryers and decentralised energy systems, state agencies are increasingly becoming early customers for technologies that may otherwise struggle to find a sufficiently large market. The trend suggests that public procurement is beginning to play a market-creation role for parts of the solar industry that sit outside the mainstream photovoltaic business. Maharashtra: Building a catalogue of unconventional solar applications Maharashtra provides perhaps the clearest example of this approach. The Maharashtra Energy Development Agency (MEDA) issued an expression of interest in 2025 to discover benchmark costs for a very wide range of renewable-energy equipment and components. The list went far beyond conventional rooftop and utility-scale solar. It included floating solar, solar water heaters, parabolic-dish concentrating solar cooking systems, solar fencing kits, decentralised solar microgrids, solar-wind hybrid systems, solar dryers, solar desalination systems, solar cookers, solar-powered water purifiers, solar charkhas, solar-powered mobile charging stations, solar cooling systems and several other products. The exercise effectively creates a reference-price and procurement framework for technologies that do not yet have the same depth of market as mainstream PV. The breadth of the list is significant because it indicates that the state is not viewing solar simply as electricity generation. It is looking at solar as a technology platform that can provide heat, drying, cooking, water treatment, lighting, mobility and other decentralised services. MEDA has subsequently moved from benchmarking towards actual procurement in some applications. In 2024, for example, it tendered for solar steam cooking systems designed to serve 2,600 people across several State Reserve Police Force facilities in Maharashtra. The tender included design, manufacture, supply, installation, testing, commissioning and five years of comprehensive maintenance, with an estimated value of around ₹3.27 crore. In 2026, MEDA also floated a tender for a solar steam cooking system using a Scheffler-dish concentrator for daily lunch and dinner for 500 people at an SRPF facility in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. The estimated tender value was about ₹65.8 lakh. Different Model of Solar Deployment Another 2026 MEDA tender combined a solar cooking system for 630 people with 4,000 litres per day of solar water-heating capacity at SRPF camps in Nagpur and Chandrapur. This is a different model of solar deployment from the conventional module-and-inverter market. The government is effectively becoming the anchor customer for a technology because the technology solves a specific institutional problem — in this case, reducing conventional fuel use for large-scale cooking and hot-water requirements. Solar cooking is particularly suited to this model. MNRE itself identifies institutional kitchens, residential schools, hospitals, police and armed-forces kitchens, hotels and religious institutions as potential applications for solar cookers. It notes that community solar cookers can save around 35–40 LPG cylinders a year when fully utilised. Telangana: From solar electricity to solar heat and storage Telangana offers another example of the diversification of solar procurement. TGREDCO has been procuring solar water-heating systems for institutional applications. In August 2025, it invited bids for 18 systems of 1,000 litres per day and three systems of 1,500 litres per day across 21 Mini Gurukulams, with five years of comprehensive maintenance. The state has also been experimenting with solar-plus-storage. In August 2025, TGREDCO invited an expression of interest for a 100 kW solar PV system paired with a 100 kW/400 kWh BESS at Cheekupally village in Mulugu district, including five years of O&M. This points to another emerging procurement pattern: instead of treating solar as a standalone generation technology, state agencies are beginning to procure it as part of a complete energy service that combines generation, storage and specific end-use requirements. Telangana has also been promoting concentrated solar thermal systems for industrial process heat. TGREDCO's documentation identifies applications across food processing, dairy, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, textiles, paper, refining and other industries where solar heat can replace or supplement conventional thermal energy. Kerala: Solar fencing becomes a public-use application Kerala demonstrates how a technology that has little relevance to conventional power offtake can still create a significant solar procurement market. The state’s forest agencies have repeatedly tendered for solar fencing to address human-animal conflict. In 2025, the Kerala Forest Department issued a tender for nearly 19 km of hanging solar fencing across several locations in the Palakkad forest division. Individual stretches included 9 km, 3 km, 2 km and 2.8 km installations. Kerala Forest Development Corporation has also floated separate tenders for solar fencing in its forest sub-units. The requirement is fundamentally different from a conventional solar project. The solar panel is not being deployed primarily to sell electricity. It is part of a self-contained electrical fencing system that provides a safety and wildlife-management function. That distinction is important. It demonstrates how solar can become economically viable when it is attached to a problem for which grid electricity or conventional infrastructure may be expensive or impractical. The trend has continued into 2026. Kerala tenders have included 3.1 km and 4.25 km solar-power fencing installations, while forest departments have also tendered for maintenance of existing solar fencing. Solar water heaters are another recurring application. In March 2026, Kerala's e-procurement system carried a tender for 300-LPD ETC-based solar water heaters at three government schools in Kannur. Uttarakhand: Solar dryers for agricultural value addition Uttarakhand provides an example from the agricultural sector. In April 2025, the state’s procurement system carried a ₹30 lakh tender for procurement of solar dryer machines. Another tender from the Centre for Aromatic Plants in Dehradun sought 15 solar dryers with a capacity of 100 kg for villages in Okhalkanda and Bhimtal blocks of Nainital district. Here, solar is being used not to generate electricity for sale but to provide a productive-use service — drying agricultural or horticultural products. That creates a different value proposition. The economic return comes from reducing drying costs, improving product quality and potentially extending shelf life, rather than from selling kilowatt-hours. A similar application has emerged in Jammu & Kashmir. In January 2025, SKUAST-K issued a tender for solar dryers and solar tunnel dryers for chilli drying at agricultural research and extension locations in Pulwama, Anantnag, Kulgam, Bandipora and Shalimar. The project was linked to the amelioration of Kashmir chilli and food, nutritional security and income generation under a NABARD-supported programme. Again, the solar technology is being deployed as a productive asset rather than a conventional power-generation asset. The larger shift: solar as a service rather than solar as electricity Taken together, these tenders point towards an important change in the way governments are thinking about solar. The first phase of India's solar expansion was largely about generating electricity at scale. The dominant procurement models were utility-scale solar parks, rooftop PV, distributed generation and, increasingly, hybrid projects. A solar cooker does not compete directly with a 500 MW solar park. A solar dryer does not require a power-purchase agreement. A solar fence is not an electricity-generation project. A solar water heater monetises avoided fuel consumption rather than electricity generation. These applications therefore require a different route to market. Government tenders can provide that route. By becoming early adopters, government departments can create reference projects, establish technical specifications, discover benchmark prices and give manufacturers an initial customer base. Once the technology has demonstrated its economics and reliability, private institutions and commercial users may become more willing to adopt it. Maharashtra's 2025 benchmark-cost exercise is particularly revealing in this regard. The state did not restrict its enquiry to conventional PV. It sought benchmark costs for dozens of emerging applications, including solar cooling, solar dryers, solar desalination, solar fencing, solar cookers, solar-powered water purification, solar charkhas, solar charging stations and decentralised microgrids. That is effectively a catalogue of potential markets waiting to be developed.

articles.title: BHEL Leadership Reset Ahead of 2027: Why Succession Will Matter for India’s Power and Manufacturing Ecosystem
articles.description: Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited is approaching an important leadership inflection point. By the beginning of March 2027, India's public-sector engineering major could have a substantially different leadership team at the top. Chairman and Managing Director K Sadashiv Murthy is scheduled to superannuate on February 28, 2027, while Director Power Tajinder Gupta is also expected to retire on the same date. Director Engineering, Research and Development S M Ramanathan is scheduled to superannuate a month earlier, on January 31, 2027. With CMD K Sadashiv Murthy and two key functional directors approaching superannuation, BHEL faces one of its most significant management transitions in recent years. The timing is crucial: the engineering giant is carrying an order book of around ₹2.4 lakh crore and has returned to strong revenue and profit growth. Meanwhile, the position of Director Human Resources has remained vacant since March 2026, with Tajinder Gupta currently holding additional charge of the HR portfolio. On the surface, these may appear to be routine leadership changes associated with superannuation in a large Central Public Sector Enterprise. But the timing gives the developments much greater significance. BHEL is entering the transition at a moment when its business momentum, project pipeline, diversification strategy and role in India's energy security ambitions are all expanding simultaneously. The leadership change, therefore, is not simply about who occupies the corner office at BHEL House. It could influence how effectively one of India's largest engineering enterprises converts an enormous order pipeline into revenues, profitability, technological capability and opportunities for thousands of suppliers, contractors and MSMEs. A Major Transition at the Top K Sadashiv Murthy assumed charge as BHEL's Chairman and Managing Director on November 1, 2023. His present appointment runs up to February 28, 2027 or until further government orders. The Public Enterprises Selection Board process for identifying his successor has already been initiated, with the Ministry of Heavy Industries publishing the CMD vacancy in May 2026. Similarly, Tajinder Gupta, who joined BHEL's board as Director Power in September 2023, has emerged as an important operational leader during a period of renewed activity in India's thermal power sector. Following the departure of Krishna Kumar Thakur from the HR portfolio in March 2026, Gupta was also given additional responsibility as Director Human Resources. BHEL's official records confirm that Thakur relinquished charge on March 19, 2026 and Gupta subsequently assumed the additional HR responsibility. S M Ramanathan represents another strategically important position in the leadership structure. An IIT Madras-trained mechanical engineer with decades of experience across BHEL's manufacturing, engineering, R&D and operational ecosystem, Ramanathan assumed charge as Director Engineering, Research and Development on April 30, 2025. His experience spans hydro turbines, steam turbines, switchgear, digital technologies, production, project functions and finance. The near-simultaneous transition across CMD, Power, R&D and HR functions creates an unusual concentration of leadership change. That is what makes succession particularly important. Why the Timing Matters: BHEL Is Carrying a ₹2.4 Lakh Crore Order Book The leadership transition is taking place against a dramatically improved operating backdrop. BHEL reported turnover of approximately ₹32,350 crore for FY2025-26, representing growth of around 18 percent over the previous year. The company received orders worth approximately ₹75,000 crore during the year, taking its outstanding order book to roughly ₹2.4 lakh crore at the end of FY2025-26. Power-sector orders alone were worth approximately ₹59,000 crore, while around ₹16,000 crore came from industrial businesses including transportation, transmission, defence, process industries and industrial equipment. BHEL also commissioned or synchronised approximately 8.9 GW of power capacity during FY2025-26. These numbers fundamentally change the leadership discussion. For a company with such a large order book, the challenge is no longer confined to winning projects. The real test is execution . A ₹2.4 lakh crore order pipeline requires extensive coordination across engineering, procurement, manufacturing, project management, construction, vendors, logistics, working capital and customer interfaces. Any prolonged leadership vacuum across key operating functions could potentially slow decision-making at precisely the stage when execution velocity becomes critical. Conversely, a well-managed transition could allow the next leadership team to inherit one of the strongest opportunity pipelines BHEL has seen in years. Profitability Has Also Started Improving Another important factor is BHEL's improving financial performance. In the April-June quarter of FY2026-27, BHEL reported consolidated net profit of approximately ₹376.7 crore compared with a loss of around ₹455.5 crore during the corresponding quarter of the previous year. Revenue from operations increased more than 40 percent year-on-year to approximately ₹7,698 crore. Significantly, the company's power business returned to profitability during the quarter. Power-segment revenue grew to about ₹5,919.5 crore, compared with ₹3,898.9 crore during the corresponding period a year earlier. This means BHEL's next leadership is unlikely to inherit a company merely attempting a turnaround. It could inherit a company entering the execution phase of that turnaround . And these are very different management challenges. Winning orders requires competitiveness. Executing a massive backlog requires project discipline, supply-chain management, working-capital control and rapid decision-making. The Next CMD Will Have Five Strategic Priorities The incoming leadership will potentially need to simultaneously manage five major priorities. First will be order execution. The company's huge order book must translate into predictable revenue and cash flow. EPC execution, vendor coordination, project closures and timely delivery will remain critical. Second will be diversification beyond conventional power equipment. BHEL has been expanding capabilities across nuclear energy, defence, transportation, transmission, hydrogen, coal gasification and other emerging technologies. The company itself has stated that it is building capabilities in areas including defence, aerospace, urban mobility, rail transportation, hydrogen and carbon capture. Third will be technology. The retirement of the Director Engineering and R&D assumes significance because BHEL is simultaneously trying to strengthen indigenous technology capabilities. The company has recently pursued partnerships in areas such as electrolyser technologies while positioning itself for emerging opportunities associated with India's clean-energy transition. BHEL announced strategic tie-ups during 2026 relating to both alkaline and PEM electrolyser systems. Fourth will be people and organisational transformation. The HR director's position has already required an additional-charge arrangement. With several senior executives approaching superannuation, succession planning below board level will also become important. For an organisation with extensive engineering and manufacturing capabilities accumulated over decades, preserving institutional knowledge while bringing younger leadership into decision-making will be essential. Fifth will be supply-chain development. And this is where the transition becomes particularly relevant to India's MSME ecosystem. Why BHEL's Leadership Transition Matters to MSMEs BHEL is much more than a large PSU operating in isolation. Behind its power plants, industrial equipment and infrastructure projects exists a significant ecosystem of equipment manufacturers, fabricators, engineering firms, component suppliers, service providers, contractors and MSMEs. A growing BHEL order book can therefore produce a multiplier effect throughout Indian manufacturing. The company's procurement system actively engages suppliers across numerous manufacturing and project categories. BHEL also encourages MSME suppliers to register on TReDS platforms for receivables financing and operates centralised procurement arrangements for several project requirements. For MSMEs, three issues will consequently be important during the leadership transition: Continuity of procurement: Large project pipelines require predictable tendering and purchase orders. Faster vendor payments: MSMEs supplying complex engineering projects depend heavily on timely cash flows. Vendor capability development: As BHEL enters higher-technology businesses such as nuclear, defence, hydrogen and advanced transmission, Indian SMEs will need support to meet increasingly sophisticated quality and certification requirements. This represents an opportunity. Instead of viewing vendors simply as suppliers, the next BHEL leadership could treat MSMEs as strategic manufacturing partners. Such an approach would strengthen both BHEL's execution capability and India's broader objective of creating deeper domestic manufacturing supply chains. Energy Security Makes BHEL Strategically Important BHEL's relevance also needs to be viewed within India's changing energy landscape. While renewable energy capacity is expanding rapidly, India's electricity requirement continues to grow. Thermal generation remains an important part of the country's energy security architecture, while nuclear power is expected to assume a larger role over the coming decades. BHEL is positioned across several parts of this transition. It retains a strong presence in thermal power equipment while simultaneously expanding into transmission, nuclear technologies, rail transportation, defence and new-energy technologies. Its own strategic outlook has identified nuclear energy as an important opportunity, especially as India works toward significantly expanding nuclear generation capacity over the longer term. The challenge for the next leadership will therefore not be to choose simply between conventional and clean energy. It will be to position BHEL across India's entire evolving energy architecture . Leadership Continuity Will Be Closely Watched The government and Public Enterprises Selection Board have already initiated processes relating to future leadership positions. The CMD vacancy was advertised during May 2026, while the post of Director Power was subsequently advertised in June. The Director HR vacancy had also been advertised earlier following the position becoming vacant in March. That advance planning becomes important because large engineering companies benefit from continuity. Strategic decisions made today can affect projects that will remain under execution for five or even ten years. Power plants, transmission systems, nuclear equipment and industrial projects do not operate according to quarterly timelines. They require institutional consistency. SMEStreet Perspective: This Is More Than a PSU Appointment Story The forthcoming leadership changes at BHEL should therefore not be viewed merely as another round of PSU appointments. They arrive at a defining stage for the company. BHEL has regained revenue momentum. Its order book has expanded dramatically. Its power business is showing signs of stronger financial performance. At the same time, the company is attempting to move deeper into new technology-led areas. The next CMD and functional directors will have to protect this momentum. The ultimate measure of success will not be the size of the order book inherited by the new leadership, but how effectively that order book gets converted into completed projects, revenues, profitability and stronger domestic manufacturing capabilities. For India's MSMEs, the transition carries another message. A stronger, faster and more technologically ambitious BHEL could become an even larger anchor customer for India's engineering SMEs, component manufacturers and industrial service providers. That makes leadership continuity at BHEL relevant not only to shareholders and policymakers but also to thousands of enterprises operating throughout India's industrial supply chain. As February 2027 approaches, the focus will naturally remain on who succeeds K Sadashiv Murthy and the other retiring directors. But the more important question will be what mandate the next leadership receives. If the mandate combines disciplined execution, technology development, supplier ecosystem expansion and aggressive diversification, BHEL's approaching leadership transition could mark not simply a change of guard — but the beginning of the company's next growth cycle.

articles.title: Abhijit Dipke ‘Resigns’ as MP CM, but when did he become Chief Minister & in what capacity did he use state symbols?
articles.description: The deaths of more than 30 tribal children in Madhya Pradesh’s Balaghat have become a serious political and public health issue. Questions are being raised over healthcare facilities, nutrition, drinking water and the response of the state administration. Amid this, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke took a swipe at the Madhya Pradesh government by posting a satirical resignation letter on social media. The unusual part was that the letter was presented as if Dipke himself was the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh. The letter said, “I tender my resignation as the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh with immediate effect,” and even thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi for giving him the opportunity to serve the people of the state. There is, of course, one basic problem with the letter, Abhijeet Dipke is not the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh. Mohan Yadav is the Chief Minister. So while the post was clearly intended as political satire, it raises a larger question about where political criticism ends and the use of official government identity begins. The question is not whether Dipke can criticise the government There should be little debate about whether Dipke has the right to question the Madhya Pradesh government. He does. In a democracy, a citizen, political activist or political party can question the government on issues affecting people. If more than 30 tribal children have died and there are concerns about healthcare and other basic facilities, asking the government to explain what happened is completely legitimate. Dipke used his post to raise several such questions. He criticised the government’s handling of the deaths and referred to healthcare, drinking water, education, electricity and nutrition. इस तरह का व्यंग्यात्मक पत्र सोशल मीडिया पर साझा करना आखिर कहां तक सही है? भारत एक लोकतांत्रिक देश है, यहां हर नागरिक को किसी भी मुद्दे पर अपनी प्रतिक्रिया रखने, सवाल पूछने और असहमति व्यक्त करने का पूरा अधिकार है। लेकिन सवाल यह है कि क्या अपनी बात रखने के लिए संवैधानिक पदों,... pic.twitter.com/xXOKpO3RtZ — NCIB Headquarters (@NCIBHQ) September 13, 2026 He also questioned the compensation announced for the families and asked whether the same amount would have been considered sufficient if the children had been the children of ministers or MLAs. These are political arguments and can be debated in the public sphere. The more interesting question, however, is why the criticism had to be presented using the identity of the Chief Minister’s office. Also Read: ‘Shariya Court’ cannot act as parallel court under Indian law: Chhattisgarh HC rejects triple talaq declaration But in what capacity was he ‘resigning’? Dipke’s letter was not simply a social media post saying that the Chief Minister should resign. It was designed to look like an official resignation letter. The post used the designation of the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh, the Chief Minister’s Office address and an official-looking government symbol. It also carried a signature, making the document look like an actual resignation letter at first glance. Dipke then used the document to make his political point. That is where the issue becomes more complicated. A person can write a satirical letter. A person can make fun of a government. A person can even write a fictional resignation letter as part of political commentary. But does that automatically give the person the right to use an official designation and government insignia to make the document look like it has come from a government office? That is the question which deserves to be asked. Imagine an ordinary young person doing the same Consider a simple example. Suppose a young person is unhappy with the functioning of the police in his district. He wants to make a political point about law and order. He creates a letter using the designation of the Superintendent of Police, adds the official address of the SP’s office and places a government emblem on the document. He then posts it on social media claiming, as a joke, that he has resigned as the district’s Superintendent of Police. Would the police department simply dismiss it as freedom of expression? Attn @MPPoliceDeptt This is gross violation of State Emblem of India (Prohibition of Improper Use) Act, 2005 Please take immediate action https://t.co/8TLKCH4cFf — Hindu IT Cell (@HinduITCell) September 13, 2026 What if another person did the same thing using the designation of a Police Commissioner, Director General of Police, District Magistrate, MLA, MP, Governor or even the President? Would the use of the official identity suddenly become acceptable because the person said it was satire? These questions are important because the standard should ideally remain the same regardless of who is making the post or which political side they support. Satire is part of democracy, but presentation also matters Political satire has always been part of democratic life. Governments and politicians are regularly mocked through cartoons, memes, parody speeches, social media posts and satirical videos. No democratic society can function properly if criticism or humour directed at those in power is treated as unacceptable. But satire also depends on context. There is a difference between writing, “The Chief Minister should resign over this failure” and creating a document that looks like an official resignation letter from the Chief Minister’s Office. In the first case, the criticism is direct and clearly political. In the second, the person is using the identity and appearance of an official government document to make the point. That distinction matters because government symbols and official designations carry authority of their own. They are not ordinary logos or decorative elements that anyone can simply use to make a social media post look authentic. More than 30 children from the Baiga and Gond tribal communities have reportedly died amid concerns over suspected infectious diseases, including measles and [...]

articles.title: How Project Zorawar is breaking India’s tank manufacturing monopoly
articles.description: The country's state-owned defence undertakings have so far had a monopoly on the main battle tank programmes, controlling everything from design to systems integration to through-life support.Project Zorawar has changed that. While Larsen & Toubro (L&T) originally partnered with DRDO as lead system integrator to fast-track the sub-25-tonne light tank, the project has since expanded into a competitive multi-vendor ecosystem featuring Tata Advanced Systems and Mahindra Defence. This is a structural shift that analysts call a genuine turning point for India’s armoured vehicle industry, rather than just another private-sector contract win. “It definitely demonstrates competence as far as private companies are concerned in terms of system engineering, configuration management, testing, quality assurance, integration of weapons and sensors. The whole life cycle support would now be responsibility of private companies,” says Col Rajneesh Singh, PhD (Retd), Research Fellow, Defence Economics and Industry Centre, MP-IDSA.Chetan Mehta, founding partner at Aum Ventures, says: “Zorawar is really the first main battle platform where a private player held that role from design through production, rather than being brought in downstream."Also Read: Defence spending gets 15 percent lift, touches 2 percent of GDPA Ladakh-born urgencyThe trigger, according to Singh, was an operational urgency. During the 2020 Ladakh standoff, China’s Type 15 tanks, built for high-altitude terrain at roughly 33 tonnes with a power-to-weight ratio near 33 horsepower per tonne, outclassed India’s 40-tonne-plus T-72 and T-90 fleets, which manage closer to 18-19 horsepower per tonne. That mismatch created an urgent requirement for a lighter, more mobile platform, one India’s DPSU-led model was not built to deliver quickly.What followed was Project Zorawar, which moved from concept to prototype in about 2 years, a significantly high speed for the defence industry. L&T, which had already built expertise through the K9 Vajra self-propelled artillery programme, moved from order to first prototype in under 19 months, and from concept to Army trials in roughly two years. Col Rajneesh contrasts that with the MBT Arjun and the Tejas light combat aircraft, both sanctioned in the early 1980s and still not fully inducted decades later. “If you start counting in terms of years, we are almost 30 years behind,” he says while adding that while Sular in Tamil Nadu does serve as the home base for indigenously built Tejas, the subsequent upgraded aircrafts have not yet been inducted.The compression came not from cutting testing, he notes, but from running user, developer and industry in parallel from day one, reusing existing industrial capability, and iterating prototypes through trials. “So, when the first prototype was tested in desert conditions, and subsequently that prototype was taken to high altitude, the lessons from those trials were incorporated into subsequent prototypes. So, what lesson comes out is that speed came less from eliminating testing. In fact, testing moved at a rather faster pace at the earlier stages of the development, and therefore we were able to shorten the whole program compared to our experience in the past,” Singh explains.This new, faster way of building a major tank has also created opportunities further down the supply chain for smaller tech innovators.“Small tech companies don't need to build an entire tank. They can focus on just one tricky part—like electrical systems, targeting tools, radios, or smart software,” says Rishab Malik, Managing Partner at Jungle Ventures and an investor in Sanlayan Technologies, a defence startup in Bengaluru. He adds that “With the government requiring thousands of parts to be made in India and forcing companies to source up to 60 percent of their materials locally, the main tank builders must now find Indian suppliers for parts they used to import from other countries.”Yet, the real advantage in the business of defence comes from having survived years of military testing and then delivered reliably.Also Read: Graphic of the day: Private sector’s defence leapInvestors see a value-chain upgradeFor investors, that timeline is the headline number. Mehta calls the combination of a committed domestic customer and genuine IP ownership the thing that “makes defence technology investable now,” arguing it can compress timelines that used to take a decade. Kushal Bhagia Founder and Partner at All In Capital frames it as the sector moving up the value chain as private firms that once supplied components or sub-assemblies can now own design, integration and manufacturing of a complete platform, capturing a far larger share of programme value and making the businesses themselves investable at greater scale. “For investors, that creates the possibility of backing businesses that are not just vendors, but can build IP, own platforms and participate in much larger programmes over a longer period of time,” he adds.The export questionBoth investors, along with Singh, are careful to separate that credibility from an automatic export pitch. Winning a domestic order is not the same as winning a tender in the Global South, where competitiveness depends on sustained serial production of dozens to hundreds of units, a proven in-country spares and after-sales network, and pricing that beats established suppliers such as from Russia, China, Turkey, and South Korea, Mehta believes.Col Rajneesh adds that a domestic precondition for export is that Zorawar first needs to be reliably inducted into Indian armed forces and demonstrate competitive life-cycle costs before export credentials mean much at all.L&T is no longer aloneTata Advanced Systems and Mahindra Defence have both since been cleared to build their own prototypes, turning what began as a single company’s programme into a wider contest among private players for future armoured-vehicle orders. Forbes India reached out to Tata Advanced Systems and Mahindra Defence for comment on how they view the shift underway in tank manufacturing but both companies declined to comment.Also Read: Graphic of the day: India's largest defence dealsWhat Happens to DPSUsThis pivot in India’s defence manufacturing does not leave the state-owned entities such as the Heavy Vehicles Factory, Avadi, with a demotion. Both Mehta and Singh expect a bifurcated market as DPSUs anchoring legacy platforms such as Arjun variants and the T-72/T-90 fleet, plus large-volume serial production, heavy fabrication and the overhauls and mid-life upgrades that recur through a tank’s service life.Far from sidelining public infrastructure, this evolving landscape reframes the industry around performance and capability rather than ownership. “Greater competition is inevitable, and I think that is ultimately positive. Capital will increasingly move towards companies that can demonstrate better technology, execution and cost efficiency-- whether that company is public or private should become less important,” says Bhagia.The requirements driving that new generation have shifted too. Col Rajneesh describes tanks moving from a triad of armour, gun and mobility toward “an integrated network combat platform,” shaped by lessons from Ukraine and West Asia on drones, electronic warfare and unmanned teaming; Zorawar’s own programme has already folded-in loitering-munition integration. Mehta reads the same signal as a capital-allocation cue: sensor fusion, defence AI and autonomous systems, not tonnage, are becoming the real differentiator.But what of the larger military tech ecosystem? As Malik puts it, deep tech defence was never a poor investment, it was always a test of patience. “Revenue arrives slowly before it compounds, while the advantage you build becomes very hard for anyone to replicate,” he adds.Also Read: How GalaxEye's Mission Drishti can shore up defence and agricultureThe larger pictureCol Rajneesh sees Zorawar as part of a broader pattern rather than an isolated case, pointing to missile manufacturing, where Bharat Dynamics’ monopoly on conventional systems is also being opened to private players. If that reading holds, Zorawar’s real significance may lie less in the tank itself than in what it proves is now possible to build, and finance, underneath it.
